items.title: Could AI help reduce surgical backlog? Manitoba researchers are ‘very optimistic’
items.description: The University of Manitoba is exploring whether AI can reduce surgical wait times in hospitals which remain a challenge for Manitoba’s health-care system.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Guy Arnel was told he may have to wait 18 months to get hip surgery. (CTV News)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: The University of Manitoba is exploring whether AI can reduce surgical wait times in hospitals which remain a challenge for Manitoba’s health-care system.
items.body:
WINNIPEG – The University of Manitoba is exploring whether AI can reduce surgical wait times in hospitals which remain a challenge for Manitoba’s health-care system.

According to researchers, more than 1,300 people are facing the orthopedic surgery backlog, with a median wait time of 170 days. For patients living with chronic pain or limited mobility, these delays can significantly affect their quality of life.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Dr. Jay Toor, assistant professor at the Rady Faculty of Health Sciences and orthopedic surgeon at Winnipeg’s Concordia Hospital and Health Sciences Centre, is leading an initiative to develop new technology called The Operating Room Intelligence and Optimization Network, or ORION, which is an AI-powered system designed to better predict surgical needs and improve operating room scheduling.

Rather than waiting for scheduling problems to emerge, ORION aims to give hospital teams information they can use to plan ahead.

“When we ran this program at Sunnybrook Hospital in Toronto, this was like a preliminary version of it, we were able to increase efficiency up to 30 per cent; that means 30 per cent faster,” said Toor.

“You didn’t have to build any operating room. You didn’t have to hire any more staff. You’re just able to squeeze more efficiency out of this existing stuff without stressing out staff.”

The project will be tested at Manitoba’s largest hospital Health Sciences Centre (HSC).

Toor says the team will use ORION to analyze 10 years of historical patient data from HSC in the first year, which will determine how accurately the AI model would have predicted surgical demand in the past.

In the project’s second year, the team will focus on prospective testing.

“I’m very optimistic we’re going to be the first jurisdiction that uses a predicted and optimized AI model to schedule our surgeries,” he said.

Toor believes ORION could produce capacity for five to eight per cent more orthopedic surgeries and could reduce wait times by up to 15 per cent.

He also believes more efficient scheduling could save the province $2-4 million annually.

“It’s massively important,” he said.

“We have to build out more infrastructure, but what we don’t want to do is build our infrastructure that we haven’t made more efficient first, so this is an incremental step.”

“There’s going to be a lot of changes to our health system, and things are trending in the right direction,” he said.

‘Just sit and wait’

For Manitoban Guy Arnel, simply getting out of a chair and walking is a daily battle.

After dealing with years of back pain, and waiting for surgery in Manitoba, Arnel decided to take matters into his own hands and travelled to Mexico last year, where he paid around $35,000 for his much-needed procedure.

Now, not even two years later, he’s in pain once again, facing yet another lengthy wait.

He’s waiting for hip surgery and was told it could take up to 18 months in Manitoba.

“I’m still an active guy. I do lots of crazy stuff. Now I can’t do anything. Just sit and wait,” he said.

“Eighteen months, to me, is terrible to hobble around. I’m so tired of hobbling around.”

He is now once again looking out of province for surgery, but he says it will come at a cost.

“Calgary’s $30,000; Quebec’s $24,000; Ontario $30,000, but now I’ve discovered that next door, Saskatchewan is $12,000,” he said.

“So that’s what I’m working on right now to go to Regina and see what I can get done there.”

“I’m running out of money, but your health is important,” he said.

While U of M researchers are working on technology to try and reduce the ever-growing backlog, Arnel is not confident it will change anything.

“I feel like this is the way it is,” he said.

items.body:
OTTAWA - As Canada-U.S. trade talks intensify, the federal government is pushing ahead with efforts to diversify Canada’s trading relationships and attract foreign investment, with a series of international meetings and trade initiatives planned in the coming weeks, and several others that have already happened.

This week, Canada and the United Arab Emirates launched a new strategic partnership.

“A comprehensive economic partnership has been negotiated in 47 days, a new record that we will use to challenge at least the Canadian system,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said.

The announcement is the latest step in the government’s push to expand Canada’s economic relationships beyond the United States.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Carney’s diplomatic agenda has been moving quickly.

  • Oct. 21-24: Prime Minister Mark Carney’s visit to Turkiye
  • Oct. 26-27: Visit to Ottawa by the Crown Prince of Abu Shabi
  • Oct. 29-30: European Union leaders in Montreal for Canada-EU Summit
  • Nov. 2-4: Prime Minister Mark Carney’s visit to Antigua and Barbuda
  • Nov. 16-18: ASEAN Summit is being held in the Philippines. Prime Minister Mark Carney is expected to attend.
  • Nov. 18-19: APEC Summit is being held in China. Prime Minister Mark Carney is expected to attend.
  • Dec. 11-12: India’s prime minister will visit Canada

Speaking with CTV Question Period host Vassy Kapelos last week, India’s high commissioner to Canada, Dinesh K. Patnaik, suggested a trade agreement between the two countries could be finalized before Prime Minister Narendra Modi visits in December.

“We have got most of it worked out. A few nicks here and there. Some legal scrubbing. But I’m extremely confident that we will be able to achieve (a deal) much before the prime minister’s visit,” Patnaik said.

However, the Opposition Conservatives argue the government still needs to deliver on its promises.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre took aim at the government’s emphasis on international summits and signing ceremonies, saying Canadians are still waiting for tangible results.

“Someday over the rainbow, if we just follow it, we might get to a pot of gold,” Poilievre said in the House of Commons, criticizing what he described as repeated announcements and photo opportunities.

International trade expert Stuart Trew also questioned whether the government’s approach risks prioritizing the number of agreements pursued over their substance.

“There’s an angle to this trade agenda that to me just looks a bit like free trade bingo, like it kind of looks like they’re just hitting a piece of paper and figuring out who wants to sign a trade agreement with us,” Trew said.

Carney has set a goal of attracting $1 trillion in investment over the next five years. The federal budget, which will be unveiled Tuesday, is expected to include measures intended to help the government reach that target.

While the government pursues new trade partnerships, a breakthrough in Canada-U.S. trade talks has yet to take shape.

items.body:
Canada and the European Union have pledged to deepen their security, digital and scholastic relationships, pushed by what they’ve described as a destabilized international order.

The two-day EU-Canada Summit wrapped up Friday after months of speculation around how a new alliance between the two bodies will take shape. Prime Minister Mark Carney, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa were involved in talks. On Friday afternoon, they released a joint statement.

All three have said they would like to see Canada become an “associate member” of the bloc. Some countries, led by Germany, have bristled at that term. Conservatives called the summit a distraction.

items._ogDesc: Ottawa has designated a multi-billion-dollar “mega project” in Metro Vancouver as a project of national interest.
items.body:
DELTA — Ottawa has designated a multi-billion-dollar “mega project” in Metro Vancouver as a project of national interest.

The federal government has said the Port of Vancouver’s planned Roberts Bank Terminal 2 expansion will bring thousands of jobs and help strengthen our country’s trade sovereignty.

Minister of Transport, Steve MacKinnon, said the announcement provides greater regulatory certainty to help advance a critical infrastructure project while maintaining rigorous environmental safeguards.

He also said the port is approaching the current port is approaching the limit of its container handling capacity.

“We can not afford to let bottlenecks hold back Canadian trade. We need the capacity to move more goods, reach more markets and seize new opportunities, and RBT2 is an important part of that solution,” he said during a news conference.

The proposed 3-berth container terminal would add 2.4 million units of annual container capacity, increasing capacity at the Port of Vancouver by nearly 50 per cent.

“The project represents an estimated capital investment of $5.9 billion, and where I come from, that’s a mega project,” the minister said.

B.C. premier-elect, Lorne Doerkson, also welcomed the news.

“The project is expected to generate thousands of jobs, of course, during construction, and support thousands more long-term positions across transportation, logistics, retail and manufacturing sectors,” he said.

“These are jobs that will support families, strengthen our communities and contribute billions of dollars to our economic activity over the life of the project,” Doerkson said.

Tsawwassen First Nation had fought for assurances around environmental protections, and said Canada has committed to upholding those.

Tsawwassen First Nation Chief Laura Cassidy also said that, “Looking ahead, one of TFN’s highest priorities is to advance a breach in Roberts Bank causeway to improve access to habitat for young salmon.”

Ottawa has said it is investing nearly two billion dollars in environmental protection, including to protect Pacific salmon and Southern Resident Killer Whales.

But the Wilderness Committee said that’s not enough, saying the project puts the survival of the whales at risk.

“Those adverse effects will still be there, those adverse effects are science-based, and nothing can mitigate the endangerment of the southern resident orcas because of this project,” said Wilderness Committee spokesperson Lucero Gonzalez.

“We feel heartbroken, but we don’t feel defeated. We will continue to find avenues to fight this project.”

Friday’s announcement is expected to accelerate the project by up to four years, meaning it could be up and running by 2035.

items.body:
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said Friday that four oil tankers, including one carrying more than two million barrels of oil, hit mines and caught fire while travelling through the Strait of Hormuz.

Meanwhile, Yemeni authorities said Houthi rebels struck Aden, without causing any casualties, and Qatari mediators have returned to Tehran for talks with Iranian officials.

Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Friday:

Read our full coverage here

Iran says supertanker struck mine and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said Friday that a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of oil struck a naval mine and caught fire while using an unauthorized route in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media reported. The Guard said it was the fourth oil tanker to suffer an explosion Friday after attempting to use unauthorized routes through the strait.

Iran has repeatedly warned vessels against passing through the strait without Tehran’s permission. It has claimed responsibility for attacks on ships and said last month that vessels attempting to pass through the strait without authorization would face “destruction.” Tehran has asserted control over much of the waterway since the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Feb. 28.

Earlier on Friday, the Guard’s navy said three other tankers caught fire after striking mines in the strait, Iranian state TV reported. It claimed the vessels had switched off their navigation and positioning systems and ignored repeated radio warnings. Iran’s report did not identify the vessels or provide details about the crews. The Associated Press could not verify those claims.

Meanwhile, Oman said it had evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged tanker that was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz, 1.6 nautical miles off the coast of Musandam Governorate, catching fire. It is unclear whether that incident is related to the fires described by Iran.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre also reported Friday that a vessel was struck by an “unknown projectile” south of Lavan, an island just off mainland Iran near Shidvar. The organization, part of the British military that monitors maritime safety, said the crew was safe.

Yemen’s Houthis said to strike Aden

Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen attacked the port city of Aden with ballistic missiles on Friday, the spokesman for Yemen’s Saudi-backed military said, as fighting has escalated between the Iran-backed group and the Saudi-led coalition in the latest front in the Iran war.

Col. Majed al-Nazili said in a statement that the missiles targeted Aden international airport, which the Houthi rebels repeatedly struck this month, as well as the palace used by Yemen’s internationally recognized government, which was also attacked weeks ago.

Ahmed Hassan, who lives near the palace, said the explosions were so loud they broke the windows.

No casualties were reported, according to a government official. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. The Houthis did not immediately claim responsibility for the attacks.

The Saudi-led coalition also said Friday it intercepted and destroyed drones launched by the Houthis in the regions surrounding Mecca and Medina, Islam’s holiest cities. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree denied carrying out any operations targeting the areas.

Meanwhile, the United Nations said the number of displaced people in Yemen has surpassed 281,000, adding that “the crisis is spreading rather than stabilizing.”

Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on Friday for talks with Iranian officials

Iranian state media said Friday that Qatari mediators have returned to Iran for talks with officials, in the latest diplomatic push to try to broker an end to the war with the U.S. and Israel. The IRNA state news agency said the Qatari delegation was headed by the country’s foreign minister and senior adviser to the prime minister. It said they were meeting with senior Iranian officials but did not specify who.

The visit follows outreach from U.S. Vice-President JD Vance, who sent a letter in recent days to Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council. Tehran on Thursday acknowledged receipt of the letter but said it had not responded and did not detail its contents.

U.S. President Donald Trump suggested the letter was not about peace negotiations but instead about possibly allowing humanitarian aid.

Diplomats say U.S. officials have told Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action against Iran after next week’s midterm elections in the United States.

Greece blasts Libya-Turkiye maritime agreement

Greece’s prime minister rejected a maritime agreement between Libya and Turkiye, which slices ownership of part of the eastern Mediterranean Sea between the two countries.

Prime ⁠Minister ⁠Kyriakos Mitsotakis said it violates international law and should be considered null and void, and disregards the rights of Greek islands that lie between the Turkish and Libyan coasts.

The agreement, ratified by Libya’s parliament last week, revives a dispute with Egypt, Greece and Cyprus over rights in the eastern Mediterranean.

Speaking to participants of the Manama Dialogue, an annual security forum in Bahrain, via video link from New York, Mitsotakis called it a “preposterous agreement.” He called on the countries to find a solution “mutually acceptable” to the other nations that hug that section of the Mediterranean.

Israeli forces demolished two homes of Palestinian gunmen who attacked soldiers

Israeli forces demolished two homes in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron on Friday belonging to Palestinian gunmen who carried out an attack last week that killed two Israeli soldiers and wounded three others. Israel launched a sweeping military operation following the attack last week, killing both gunmen, and ordered residents to evacuate the gunmen’s neighbourhood and closed roads into and out of Hebron.

The UN humanitarian office said earlier this week that more than 3,000 people had been displaced by Israeli forces, with closures disrupting businesses and movement throughout the city.

UN human rights chief Volker Turk warned earlier this week that the operation raised grave concerns about unnecessary and disproportionate use of force. He said statements by senior Israeli officials indicated the measures were punitive and designed to instill fear, and called for displaced residents to be allowed home. “Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law,” he said.

The Associated Press

items.title: CTV News went to Kentucky to see if Canada’s bourbon bans are hurting them. Their response was blunt
items.description: Bourbon is a way of life in Bardstown, Ky. The town of more than 13,000 people, located about an hour from Louisville, is known as the bourbon capital of the world.

items.body:
BARDSTOWN, Ky. — Bourbon is a way of life in Bardstown, Ky. The town of more than 13,000 people, located about an hour from Louisville, is known as the bourbon capital of the world.

Kentucky distillers were hit hard in March 2025 when Canadian provinces pulled American alcohol and spirits off the shelves in response to U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs. Most still have the ban in place.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

“Suddenly that was a revenue stream that we had just overnight lost and we’re still trying to get it back,” said Tom Bard, co-founder of the Bard Distillery and a direct descendent of one of the brothers who founded the town in 1780.

Bard and his wife Kim opened their distillery in Graham, Ky. in 2019. They sold their products in British Columbia and Alberta, and they had plans to expand. The tariffs changed all of that.

  • CTV News asked Georgia voters about tariffs. Their answer was clear

“We’re just getting caught up in it and we’re suffering for it,” said Bard.

“I keep telling people, ‘stop the roller coaster,’ let us get off because we’re caught up in the middle of this on again, off again thing and we can’t predict our income,” Kim Bard added.

They’ve recently opened a satellite tasting room in Bardstown to make up for lost revenue.

“It’s been huge for us because it has created a whole new revenue stream,” Tom Bard said. “We’re doing what a lot of businesses are doing right now with the tariffs and other issues going on globally. And even in America, trying to get to other states with our products, spirits specifically. We are now focusing on our home market.”

The decision by the provinces to ban the sale of American alcohol and spirits meant distillers lost access to one of their largest trading partners.

According to the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States, U.S. spirits exports to Canada have fallen from US$232 million a year before the ban to US$72 million, representing a 70 per cent decline.

Kentucky bourbon and other Kentucky whiskies exported to Canada dropped 42.4 per cent last year, going from US$43.7 million in 2024 to US$25.2 million in 2025, according to the Kentucky Distiller’s Association.

“We’re not just talking about the whiskey in the bottle, we’re talking about the entire supply chain being impacted,” said Michael Bilello, the president and CEO of the American Whiskey Association.

“We have to be able to predict. We have to be able to forecast how much whiskey you need in the future because it takes years, as you know, to age. But we’ve got to get back to business. Remain hopeful that talks will continue, and we hope to put this behind us very soon.”

While the Bards have their satellite tasting room up and running, they’re also hitting the pause button on other expenses.

“We no longer get to hire people that we needed to hire. Construction projects that we’re working on, trying to expand, we had to stop them,” Tom Bard said.

They hope a trade deal between the U.S. and Canada would see the return of the flagship American export back on Canadian shelves soon.

“Anytime there is any type of a trade war going on between countries, it just creates a snowball effect that’s hard to stop,” Tom Bard said. “Getting caught up in it is just hurting people on both sides of the border.”

items.body:
TORONTO — Canada’s main stock index fell more than 600 points Friday as markets worry the frenzy around tech stocks has sent prices too high.

“For the Canadian stock market, we are borrowing the move from the U.S. stock market. It’s as simple as that,” said Sébastien Mc Mahon, chief economist at iA Financial Group.

The S&P/TSX composite index was down 629.00 points at 35,620.03.

  • Real-time TSX market updates here

Worries are rising about whether all those hundreds of billions of dollars spent on AI will produce enough profit and productivity to make the investment worth it.   

“The theme has become speculative. It’s not a bubble; we’re not that worried about valuations yet, but the market is looking for solid signals or solid information,” Mc Mahon said. 

“When we have the Anthropic IPO behind us, then we’ll have solid audited and regular information about AI adoption, but the market seems to be blindsided now by the news like we’ve had from Google and from Amazon and from Intel.” 

Anthropic filed paperwork Monday for its IPO, setting it up for a potential debut next month.

Amazon fell 1.4 per cent after reporting a weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected. A day earlier, Alphabet’s stock dropped more than 12 per cent to its worst day on record after telling investors it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring. 

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

The Dow Jones industrial average was down 572.25 points at 51,770.31. The S&P 500 index was down 140.32 points at 7,580.07, while the Nasdaq composite was down 747.73 points at 25,437.00.

Meanwhile, earnings season is also underway.

“So far so good. It’s very early, but we have a strong start,” David Caron, a portfolio manager of North American equities at iA Global Asset Management, said in a statement.

He added that investors are “desperately looking for hard data on the adoption and progress of AI” and appear to be focusing more on negative surprises. 

On Wednesday, the Bank of Canada raised its benchmark interest rate for the first time in more than three years as it tries to get ahead of looming price hikes. The central bank’s policy rate now stands at 2.5 per cent following a quarter-point hike.

Mc Mahon said the move was largely expected by investors. 

“We don’t think it was necessary, but it’s more about the waiting scheme so the bank is looking at inflation broadening to other components outside of gasoline,” he said.   

Going forward, signs that economic growth stalled over the summer have some economists debating the timing of the Bank of Canada’s next interest rate hike. Statistics Canada said Friday that real gross domestic product was essentially unchanged for a second straight month in August, falling short of economists’ expectations.

  • Latest updates on investing here

Looking ahead to next week, Mc Mahon said he will be watching the federal budget closely on Thursday.

“I don’t know if (the federal government) still has some dry powder. They announced quite a bit since the budget of the last year,” he said. 

Prime Minister Mark Carney has been focused on an aggressive infrastructure agenda to build the economy in the face of U.S. tariffs and geopolitical changes.  

The Canadian dollar traded for 71.63 cents US compared with 71.51 cents US on Thursday.  

The December crude oil contract was up US$2.12 at US$104.12 per barrel.

The December gold contract was down US$132.50 at US$3,898.90 an ounce. 

Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press

items.title: Canada, European Union close Montreal summit with ‘alliance for the future’ pact
items.description: Mark Carney and his European Union counterparts closed a major summit Friday by announcing what they called an 'alliance for the future.'
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Prime Minister Mark Carney, centre, arrives at the EU-Canada summit with President of the European Council, Antonio Costa, left, and President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, in Montreal on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Christopher Katsarov]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu"></media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Mark Carney and his European Union counterparts closed a major summit Friday by announcing what they called an 'alliance for the future.'
items.body:
MONTREAL — Canada and the European Union officially launched an “alliance for the future” on Friday and pledged to spend the next eight months in negotiations on making Canada an associate member — despite objections to that language on both sides of the Atlantic.

“Today we move toward associate membership for Canada and we launch a new alliance for the future,” Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters Friday.

He was speaking at a news conference closing a two-day summit in Montreal with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.

Both jurisdictions released a seven-page joint statement Friday that calls for more industrial collaboration and supply chain integration and cites various current joint projects.

The statement included announcements that officials on both sides of the Atlantic promoted in the days leading up to the Montreal summit.

They include a new digital trade agreement and a deal to allow the European Investment Bank to fund critical raw materials projects in Canada.

Carney said the various agreements signed Friday will make it easier for Canadians to do business with and within the EU.

“Seamless payments will make it easier to sell online in Europe, so a business owner in Manitoba or a lobster harvester in Prince Edward Island will clear customs faster, getting their products to European markets,” Carney said.

“A tech startup in Vancouver will have a smoother path to customers in Berlin. Bottom line, less red tape, more growth, more opportunity.”

Carney argued these agreements will help make life more affordable for Canadians.

Carney also announced Canada would join an EU loan program for Ukraine, with Ottawa pledging an initial contribution of 500 million euros, roughly $775 million.

Von der Leyen said the agreements signed Friday will help create “good jobs” and encourage companies to expand.

The joint statement also cites agreements to give Canadian artificial-intelligence researchers access to European supercomputers and to hold more discussions on Arctic and border security.

The statement calls for reforming the World Trade Organization instead of replacing it, and doing more to fight climate change and biodiversity loss.

Carney said he and the other leaders discussed resolving the prospect of Canadian goods being affected by the EU’s anti-deforestation law and its Carbon Border Adjustment Measures, which tariff imports to match European pollution pricing.

A Canadian government official speaking on background said there is more work to do on getting European institutions to recognize what Canada is doing federally and provincially to price emissions. The official said those talks are very advanced.

The agreement also pledges to “explore a next-generation youth mobility partnership” touching on work and academic exchanges.

Von der Leyen said the goal is to have Canada fully join Erasmus+, the EU’s student exchange program that offers training and study opportunities in member nations.

A Canadian government official said the goal is for Canada to join Erasmus+ midway through 2027. The program is paid for by member states and has a 2021 to 2027 funding pool of about $41 billion.

The official said Canada also wants to become a full member of the Horizon Europe program by 2028. Canada is already a second-tier member of Horizon, which funds research and innovation projects.

Costa said Thursday he wants to see this partnership expand labour mobility between Canada and Europe.

All three leaders discussed the prospect of Canada obtaining “associate member” status in the EU, despite strong pushback from member states, including Germany.

The leaders announced Friday that Carney will next spring join a meeting of von der Leyen’s cabinet — the college of commissioners — and that Costa will host Carney in June at a meeting of the European Council.

Costa said the goal is to announce more details of the partnership at that June meeting.

Culture Minister Marc Miller said Thursday any discussions of labour mobility in industries like film production would need to include the provinces, many of which have their own tax credits that promote local talent.

Miller has been meeting with his European counterparts to discuss setting new regulations on promoting Canadian and European content on streaming services, along with new safeguards for children online.

“We’re not talking about the same exact rules potentially, but convergence and allyship with respect to large, transnational companies that in some cases need to be regulated to protect kids or to promote our cultures in the face of overwhelming, monopolistic cultures, one of which is the United States, but others across the world,” Miller said in an interview.

Conservatives have criticized this week’s summit, noting that nine of the 28 countries in the EU have yet to ratify a decade-old trade deal with Canada known as CETA. They also want the EU to stop charging a carbon tariff on certain Canadian imports.

“Worse, there was lots of talk at the summit about aligning Canada with the insane European taxes, debt, immigration and anti-oil and gas policies that have left parts of Europe bankrupt and burning,” Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said in a statement on social media.

“Does any of this lower your mortgage payments, rent, grocery bills or gas prices, back here in the real world? Of course not. Time to get real. We have mouths to feed. Bills to pay. Crime to stop. Borders to secure. And money to save.”

The Bloc Québécois said Carney must fulfil a promise to hold a vote on the new arrangements with the EU.

“This new alliance and this status, about which we know very little, must absolutely be negotiated with Quebec,” the party wrote in French, noting Friday’s announcements touch on provincial jurisdiction.

With files from Dylan Robertson in Ottawa

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A transport truck carries a cargo container at the Port of Vancouver, on Friday, July 14, 2023. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Darryl Dyck]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">DARRYL DYCK</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: TFI International Inc. reported its net income rose to US$105.7 million in the third quarter from US$84.7 million a year earlier.
items.body:
MONTREAL — Higher profits and revenue failed to keep TFI International’s stock from sinking Friday as investors focused instead on the company’s earnings miss, a disappointing forecast and a major contract loss.

The country’s largest trucking firm saw its share price drop 17 per cent to close at $130.05 on the Toronto Stock Exchange.

The decrease came after its net income and adjusted earnings fell short of expectations and its fourth-quarter outlook underwhelmed analysts.

  • Latest updates on company news here

“You have inflation like we went through in Q2 and in Q3 with fuel, that turns to be more of a negative,” said CEO and chairperson Alain Bédard.

He was talking specifically about less-than-truckload (LTL) shipments, which see multiple drops of cargo for different clients on a single run, in the United States. There, the company has a farther-flung network and less efficient routes than in Canada.

“We do about 20,000 shipments a day. We cover all of the U.S. and our density is not good,” he said.

Pricing in the segment marks another area of concern.

“It’s not the market that’s the problem, it’s us. We have to do a better job commercially to identify what fits,” Bédard said.

“We’ve been going through a very rough patch in our U.S. LTL for the year,” he summarized. “We’re not very happy at all with the results.

“We believe that we’re going to turn the corner in 2027.”

Some analysts cast doubt on that prospect.

“Inadequate pricing and lack of density mentioned on the call do not in our view sound like easy fixes,” said analyst Walter Spracklin of RBC Dominion Securities in a note to investors.

He also pointed to the newly announced loss of a US$300-million contract with shipping giant UPS, “which explains the market reaction today.”

However, analyst Benoit Poirier said weakness in the company’s less-than-truckload segment “overshadowed solid execution” from its full truckload and logistics divisions.

TFI’s net income jumped 25 per cent year-over-year to US$105.7 million last quarter. Revenue at the Montreal-based company, which keeps its books in U.S. dollars, rose 13 per cent to US$2.23 billion.

  • Latest updates on investing here

South of the border, an immigration crack down on commercial truck drivers has had varied effects on shipping carriers. The demand for licensing data by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Transportation has forced the closure of some driver training schools and pushed out drivers who have valid licenses but may also be undocumented.

The result is less competition as some firms have shuttered, but also higher wages for workers.

“We have pressure on labour costs. Why is that? Because everybody is looking for drivers,” Bédard said.

“That brings inflation to the salary, which between you and me I think is needed,” he said.

“We have to push customers around that this is the new reality, my friend, and this is the new price. We’re not in the business of practising delivery just to have fun.”

On an adjusted basis, diluted earnings leaped 39 per cent to US$1.67 per share in the three months ended Sept. 30 from US$1.20 per share in the same period a year earlier. But the outcome fell below analysts’ expectations of US$1.76 per share.

TFI’s adjusted profit forecast of between US$1.30 and US$1.40 per share in its fourth quarter also notched well beneath analyst predictions of roughly US$1.65.

Christopher Reynolds, The Canadian Press

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

items._ogDesc: New Brunswick’s Crown-owned electric utility is being criticized for changing its policy on the sale of excess power.
items.body:
FREDERICTON — One of Canada’s largest forestry companies is accusing New Brunswick’s public utility of giving preferential treatment to outside industrial customers.

Earlier this year, a provincial regulator gave permission for NB Power to sell cheaper surplus power at market rates to out-of-province customers in a move that could boost the utility’s revenues by millions of dollars.

The regulator’s ruling allowed the utility to prioritize fixed sales contracts with external customers instead of offering discounted surplus rates to local manufacturers.

This would be a departure from the utility’s practices in previous decades, when it sold excess electricity to several large customers in the province at a discount before exporting power.

While the province’s big manufacturers buy some electricity at a fixed rate from NB Power, many are also able to save on energy costs by buying surplus power at a discount.

NB Power says it uses revenues from sales outside of New Brunswick to help offset the cost of providing electricity service to regular customers inside the province.

A statement from the Crown corporation said it “sought changes to better align the price of interruptible energy with the cost of providing this variable product,” referencing excess power sales.

Mark Mosher, an executive at forestry giant J.D. Irving Ltd., alleges that, by prioritizing export contracts, NB Power is selling what was previously the cheap surplus power to external customers in the United States and other provinces.

That forces J.D. Irving and other large-scale industrial customers to purchase more expensive excess power at a higher rate, Mosher told The Canadian Press.

NB Power in a statement late Friday denied selling U.S. customers surplus energy.

“We are not selling hourly export products to anyone before we serve all load, including interruptible power, in New Brunswick,” NB Power said.

A spokesperson did not immediately respond to a question about whether it was selling what was previously the cheap surplus power it sold to local industrial customers to external customers for more money.

Local manufacturers say their costs are rising after losing access to the cheap surplus power.

Mosher said the policy change could drive up power costs for J.D. Irving Ltd. subsidiary Irving Paper by an estimated $10 million annually and cause it to close.

The move “will have devastating consequences” for large manufacturers already facing high rates if it’s not reversed, Mosher said in a statement earlier this month.

J.D. Irving has asked the New Brunswick Energy and Utilities Board to review the decision, arguing that major employers were not notified of the proposal when the regulator approved the changes in April.

Meanwhile, provincial Energy Minister Rene Legacy says the surplus market pricing benefits NB Power’s fixed electricity customers, including residents, as the corporation is able to find profit elsewhere.

“We could reverse this, and it could be changed, but somebody else would be impacted,” Legacy said in New Brunswick’s legislature on Tuesday.

He added the Liberal government won’t intervene in J.D. Irving Ltd.’s application to the power board.

Jennifer Murray, who as Atlantic regional director for Unifor represents more than 3,000 unionized forestry workers in New Brunswick, says the surplus power change only adds to the economic pressures the forestry sector is already facing.

“In the middle of a trade war, it’s not a wise decision to be selling anything to the United States before looking at taking care of New Brunswickers first,” Murray said in an interview.

She said higher power bills for J.D. Irving, AV Group NB, Twin Rivers Paper Company and other big forestry manufacturers will lead to layoffs and shutdowns, as it has in the past.

Mosher, who is vice president of J.D. Irving’s pulp and paper division, said he’s all too familiar with the relationship between power costs and job losses.

Last year, Irving Paper closed one of its two paper machines and laid off 140 workers in February 2025, blaming a 10 per cent industrial electricity rate increase at the time.

“Successive NB Power rate hikes have resulted in a 38 per cent increase over the last four years, with an additional 17 per cent requested over the next three years, further entrenching an already uncompetitive business landscape,” Mosher said.

“The situation has become untenable, and we know where this leads.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

Eli Ridder, The Canadian Press

items.title: Why mortgage brokerages should attend the CMAs as a team
items.description: The CMAs are Canada's top mortgage industry night — and the ROI extends well beyond individual recognition
items.content: <p>The CMAs are Canada's top mortgage industry night — and the ROI extends well beyond individual recognition</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0270_637746489857378440.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The CMAs are Canada's top mortgage industry night — and the ROI extends well beyond individual recognition
items.body:
For mortgage brokers and brokerage leaders across Canada, the Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs) have long represented the industry's highest standard of professional recognition.

Now in their 20th year, the CMAs are set to take place on November 25 at Rebel Toronto — and this milestone edition makes a compelling case for attending not as an individual, but as a team.

While individual nominations drive the night's agenda, the strategic value of group attendance at the CMAs extends far beyond the trophy.

For brokerages thinking seriously about recruitment, retention, culture, and competitive positioning, booking a table, or a block of seats, is increasingly less a luxury and more a sound business decision.

The case for a team night out

Mortgage brokerage is, at its core, a people business. The culture a firm builds internally — how it celebrates wins, how it acknowledges hard work, how it signals that individual effort is seen — has a direct effect on retention.

In an industry where top brokers face constant competition for their services, that culture gap can be costly.

Attending the CMAs as a group is one of the more tangible ways a brokerage can make that message concrete.

The event's November 25 evening at Rebel Toronto begins with a cocktail reception from 6:00 p.m. to 7:30 p.m., followed by the awards ceremony and dinner banquet until 10:30 p.m., with a post-awards celebration running well into the night.

It is not a brief industry function — it is a full evening designed, in the words of the organizers, for sharing insights, networking and building connections.

For a brokerage principal, bringing a group of agents or support staff signals something that a memo cannot: that their contributions are worth celebrating in public, before their peers, in the same room as hundreds of the foremost mortgage professionals and key executives from top Canadian organizations.

Secure a table at the 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards and celebrate your team’s achievements alongside industry leaders, innovators, and top-performing professionals from across the country. #MortgageAwardsCA Book your table today: https://t.co/SSKx4yuft5 https://t.co/f31Lgyrrzt — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 28, 2026

Recognition that reaches beyond the individual

The CMAs span 26 award categories, recognising brokers, brokerages, lenders, business development managers, underwriters, and service providers across the Canadian mortgage industry.

Across those categories, the awards are designed to reflect not just individual performance but the collective effort behind it.

When a broker wins, or is named an excellence awardee ahead of the November gala, the recognition lands in Canadian Mortgage Professional (CMP) magazine and across its online channels.

The profiles and features generated from shortlistings and wins carry the names of those firms into editorial content that reaches CMP's readership throughout the year. For a brokerage, that coverage is institutional: it attaches to the firm's brand, not only to the individual.

That makes the case for corporate attendance straightforward. A team present in the room when a colleague is recognised associates the brokerage with the win in a way that a congratulatory email the next morning cannot replicate.

The CMAs have been described by past winners, including Steven Ranson of HomeEquity Bank in Toronto, as "iconic" — an event where the industry turns out to take stock of itself. Being part of that moment, collectively, carries a different weight than watching it from outside.

For brokerages that have not yet submitted a nomination, the deadline has passed for the 2026 cycle, with excellence awardees already announced in September.

But the event itself remains open to the industry, and registering as a group for the CMAs gala at Rebel Toronto is a separate matter from the nomination process.

The networking case for corporate attendance

Beyond recognition, the CMAs function as one of the most concentrated networking events on the Canadian mortgage calendar.

Hundreds of senior professionals — brokers, lenders, aggregators, and executives — gather in a single venue for an evening built around industry conversation.

The cocktail reception that opens the night is specifically designed to facilitate that kind of contact before the formal programme begins.

For a junior broker or an agent new to the industry, attending the CMAs alongside experienced colleagues offers a different kind of access.

The introductions that happen organically in rooms like Rebel Toronto — between a new agent and a business development manager from a major lender, or between a brokerage's team and a potential referral partner — are not easily manufactured in any other setting.

A group presence makes those introductions more natural: arriving as a team, rather than alone, lowers the social friction of a large industry event.

For mortgage professionals seeking deeper insight into how Canada's top brokerages and lenders benchmark their performance, events like the CMAs serve as a live read on where the industry's weight is shifting — which firms are growing, which categories are most competitive, and which names are emerging.

That intelligence, absorbed in a room with peers, is harder to replicate through trade coverage alone.

The CMA organizers note that the event "provides the ideal setting for an evening tailor-made for sharing insights, networking and building connections."

A brokerage that treats the evening as a strategic exercise, briefing its staff on who else will be in the room and what conversations are worth having, is likely to leave with more than a photograph.

Registration is open at canadianmortgageawards.com.

items.title: MCAN mortgage assets surge on strong broker originations
items.description: MCAN Financial Group grows managed assets to $9.4 billion as insured originations surge 27%
items.content: <p>MCAN Financial Group grows managed assets to $9.4 billion as insured originations surge 27%</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639289830664715117.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: MCAN Financial Group grows managed assets to $9.4 billion as insured originations surge 27%
items.body:
MCAN Mortgage Corporation d/b/a MCAN Financial Group, Canada’s federally regulated mortgage investment corporation (MIC), reported a 21% rise in total assets under management to $9.4 billion for the nine months ended September 30.

Strong residential mortgage originations, expanding securitization activity, and steady broker-driven renewals each contributed to the result.

Net interest income for Q3 2026 rose 12% to $26.7 million compared with Q3 2025.

Year-to-date net income climbed 16% to $66.2 million, underpinned by higher lending volumes and income from MCAP Commercial LP, the company’s strategic partner.

Quarterly net income declined 6% to $19.2 million on unrealized losses in MCAN’s securities portfolio.

Broker-driven volumes lift residential mortgage assets

Residential mortgage assets reached $5.1 billion at September 30, up 11% year to date. Insured assets grew 13% to $3.7 billion; uninsured assets rose 8% to $1.4 billion.

Against the same nine months of 2025, insured originations surged 27% and uninsured originations rose 13%, building on MCAN’s expanding origination base through the first half of 2026, when second-quarter net income jumped 19%.

“Strong growth in our assets under management reflects the continued execution of our strategy,” said Derek Sutherland, chief executive officer of MCAN Financial Group.

“Our business continues to perform well in all our main product lines, despite uncertainty in the broader economic environment, supported by strong mortgage originations and renewals, disciplined pricing and hedging strategies, as well as our strategic partnership with MCAP. We believe we are well-reserved in our allowance for credit losses and our sound underwriting practices ensure our credit quality remains resilient.”

That resilience is built on the broker channel. Speaking in a recent Canadian Mortgage Professional roundtable examining Canada’s evolving alternative lending landscape for mortgage brokers, Avish Buck, senior vice-president and chief operating officer of MCAN Financial Group and president of MCAN Home Mortgage Corp in Toronto, said: “When a broker works with MCAN, it means they trust us with their client, and that’s something we take seriously. Trust is the core of any relationship.”

Construction mortgages rise 9%, but impairments climb

Construction and commercial mortgage balances grew 9% year to date to $1.3 billion, with loan advances of $359 million through September 30.

Project extensions tied to permitting and zoning delays, as well as a more cautious economic environment, have affected parts of the portfolio.

The impaired non-securitized mortgage ratio rose to 2.31% from 1.69% at December 31, 2025, driven by construction loans and uninsured residential mortgages under asset recovery.

Provisions for credit losses totalled $5.7 million year to date. Average loan-to-value ratios of 68.2% on uninsured residential mortgages and 62.8% on construction loans point to credit quality challenges facing Canadian mortgage lenders that remain manageable for a conservatively underwritten book.

In October, MCAN launched an additional uninsured residential mortgage securitization program with a major Canadian bank to further diversify funding.

Year-to-date income from MCAP reached $27.6 million, up 8%. The board declared a fourth-quarter dividend of $0.43 per share, payable January 4, 2027 to shareholders of record December 15.

items.title: Economists flag Q3 downside as Canada’s GDP stalls in August
items.description: Three Bay Street analysts warn Q3 growth is tracking well short of the Bank of Canada’s forecast
items.content: <p>Three Bay Street analysts warn Q3 growth is tracking well short of the Bank of Canada’s forecast</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639289794928292353.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Three Bay Street analysts warn Q3 growth is tracking well short of the Bank of Canada’s forecast
items.body:
Canada’s economy delivered little in August, with real gross domestic product (GDP) essentially flat for a second consecutive month — trailing both market expectations and Statistics Canada’s preliminary estimate of 0.2% growth, raising fresh questions about the Bank of Canada’s decision to raise interest rates last week.

The August result follows a broadly flat July, marking a deceleration from the 3.3% annualized growth recorded in Canada’s second quarter of 2026.

With Statistics Canada’s advance estimate projecting a further 0.1% decline in September, Q3 GDP is now tracking at approximately 1.3% annualized, well below the Bank of Canada’s 2.0% projection in its October 2026 Monetary Policy Report (MPR).

The composition of August was mixed. Retail activity rose sharply, suggesting resilient household spending despite higher borrowing and energy costs.

Manufacturing output and engineering construction also gained, while wholesale trade, public administration, and oil and gas extraction all declined.

Statistics Canada reported no growth in August GDP and an estimated decline in September, suggesting third-quarter growth may fall short of the Bank of Canada’s expectations following its latest interest rate increase. https://t.co/CCruoYeDlc — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 30, 2026

Mixed signals for the central bank

On October 28, the Bank of Canada raised its overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.50%, its first hike since July 2023. Economists characterized the move as risk management, though softer GDP data complicates that framing.

Marc Ercolao, economist at TD Economics in Toronto, wrote that August’s result “may cast a little more doubt around the durability of the recovery heading into 2027,” noting that softer fourth-quarter momentum “raises the bar” for the Bank’s 2027 growth forecast, “particularly with trade uncertainty and higher energy costs still clouding the outlook.”

Andrew Grantham, senior economist at CIBC Economics in Toronto, offered a blunter take. August data, he wrote, showed that “all of the growth in Q3 came from the strong handoff at the end of the second quarter, and that throughout the period the economy actually stagnated.”

Greater slack, he added, should limit firms’ ability to pass through higher energy costs to consumers — capping core inflation below the Bank of Canada’s own MPR projections.

Abbey Xu, economist at RBC in Toronto, described the August composition as “somewhat better than the headline,” noting that retail resilience and engineering construction gains were consistent with an economy still expanding, “albeit unevenly and at a more moderate pace.”

What the data means for brokers

For mortgage professionals navigating Canada’s mounting 2026 mortgage renewal pressures, the Q3 shortfall arrives at a difficult moment.

Jessica Rickerby, president of the Canadian Mortgage Brokers Association of Ontario (CMBA Ontario) in Toronto, told Canadian Mortgage Professional: “While inflation is a key concern of Ontarians, so is housing affordability. The difference is that affordability is a pressing issue right now, whereas inflation is – at present – a hypothetical.”

With the next Bank of Canada rate decision on December 9, the small-business outlook for Canada’s mortgage market already signals a rougher fourth quarter, and October and November GDP prints will carry unusual weight.

items.body:
The Canadian economy has stalled, and the details offer little reassurance. Real GDP was flat in August for a second straight month, according to Statistics Canada (StatCan). Retail and credit card activity helped support output, an ominous combination as credit industry reports point to rising balances and delinquencies. The agency’s preliminary September estimate suggests that stagnation would be good news compared to what lies ahead.

Canada’s Economy Stalls For A Second Consecutive Month

Canadian economic output stalled for another month. Following a flat July, real GDP remained “essentially unchanged” in August. Just 9 of 20 industrial sectors expanded, with goods-producing industries rising 0.1% but tamed by a 0.1% drop in services. The stagnation follows massive jumps in April (+0.6%), May (+0.3%), and June (+0.4%), highlighting an abrupt and rapid loss of momentum.

Retail and Credit Card Activity Helping To Prop Up the Economy

The latest GDP report shows the economy may be living on borrowed time. One of the key areas of growth is retail output, rising 1.2% in August, led by vehicle dealers and food retailers. Also providing a boost was finance and insurance, which advanced 0.2%, with banking climbing 0.3% despite a slow mortgage market. The agency notes the growth in the latter was driven by non-mortgage lending activity, specifically credit cards.

That specific data point sounds more concerning when paired with TransUnion comments. The consumer credit reporting agency recently warned of rising balances and delinquency rates for consumers. They noted that consumers are increasingly relying on credit cards to smooth consumption. To be blunt, the read here isn’t very optimistic—consumer spending is helping to prop up the economy while borrowers increasingly rely on credit cards to make ends meet.

Canadian GDP Expected To Contract In September

Unfortunately, things are set to get worse according to the agency’s advance estimates. StatCan’s preliminary numbers point to a 0.1% drop in real GDP in September. Manufacturing and mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction are expected to lead the decline. However, the agency estimates average economic output in Q3 will still be 0.3% higher than in Q2, despite the loss of monthly momentum.

The figures also largely pre-date the latest tariff escalation. The U.S. imposed escalation only took effect in the final days of August, making September the first full month under those measures. It intensifies further as the first full month of Canada’s retaliatory tariffs won’t be seen until the October GDP data. StatCan hasn’t indicated whether its preliminary data fully captures the latest tariff escalation, leaving open the possibility of further weakness.

items.title: The BoC isn’t expecting the housing market to heat up anytime soon
items.description: Central bank sees a sluggish outlook continuing – and BMO managing director says less focus on housing wouldn’t necessarily be a bad thing
items.content: <p>Central bank sees a sluggish outlook continuing – and BMO managing director says less focus on housing wouldn’t necessarily be a bad thing</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639289754495839586.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Central bank sees a sluggish outlook continuing – and BMO managing director says less focus on housing wouldn’t necessarily be a bad thing
items.body:
The Bank of Canada doesn’t see much chance of a hotter national housing market in the near future, forecasting this week that housing will contribute essentially nothing to national economic growth in the next two years.

The central bank said in the latest Monetary Policy Report, released alongside its rate hike on Wednesday, that climbing borrowing costs will send housing-related expenses higher in 2027 and 2028, while material and equipment prices will also increase as home construction and maintenance costs rise.

That’s not to say housing and mortgage professionals will notice a sudden or sharp change, with the deep freeze that’s gripped the market over the past two years showing no sign of thawing.

Benjamin Reitzes (pictured top), managing director, Canadian rates and macro strategist at Bank of Montreal (BMO), told Canadian Mortgage Professional the central bank’s 25-basis-point increase on October 28 may have a slight negative impact on the market, but that there wasn’t much momentum to stall in the first place.

“What’s notable is that you already had mortgage rates notably higher right across the curve. So the only point where they were contained was on the variable side,” he said. “At least half the activity was coming in variable, according to the data.

“So [the hike] will provide a bit more of a dampener, I think, on the margin. Of course it makes a difference – but it’s not as if housing was booming. And so there probably is a limit to how much weaker it gets.”

Why the housing market is still slow

The main culprits for the still-sluggish housing market are well known at this stage: economic uncertainty triggered by the US-Canada trade war, and inflation concerns as a result of surging fuel costs.

That trade dispute has sparked fears of job losses and a big hit to the economy since the beginning of last year, while rising inflation was one of the main reasons the Bank of Canada raised rates on Wednesday and could hike again soon.

And while home prices have slid across many markets in 2025 and 2026, Reitzes suggested that the correction may still have a while to run.

“The reality for the housing market is that affordability is still stretched. There’s still room for prices to fall – the affordability side of things needs to improve,” he said. “I think at this point, the path of least resistance is probably still toward modestly lower prices for housing and continued softness on that front. And that’s what the Bank’s expecting.”

Affordability improved in almost every major Canadian market in September, according to ratehub.ca, but that picture could be complicated if rates continue rising in the coming months.

Population dynamics are also playing their part in the market’s slowdown. The federal government dramatically upped its immigration targets in the early years of this decade, boosting demand for housing and rental units.

Those targets have been pared back substantially, a trend that’s lowered clamour for condo rentals in major markets – most notably Toronto – and contributed to the wider housing market cooldown.

The market’s torpor has also fuelled calls among some executives for an end or revision to the foreign homebuyer ban that’s been in place since the beginning of 2023, although industry views on the matter have been mixed.

Why a less intense housing market could ultimately benefit Canada

Reitzes emphasized that a less intense focus on the housing market could be a net positive in the long run for the Canadian economy.

“Population growth is not particularly strong in Canada at the moment, and so the dynamics are challenging for housing – and that isn’t necessarily the worst thing,” he said. “Housing has… gotten too much attention over the past few decades, and it’s kind of shifting the focus toward business investment and toward driving productivity growth in Canada.

“As much as people love to focus on housing, sometimes it’s not always the best use of capital for the country. So it’s not the end of the world here that we’re going a different way.”

items.title: Real estate lawyer talks enforcement, institutional money – and what’s next
items.description: Grechi Carter partner and founder on the current and coming trends in private and alternative lending
items.content: <p>Grechi Carter partner and founder on the current and coming trends in private and alternative lending</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639289674628824034.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Grechi Carter partner and founder on the current and coming trends in private and alternative lending
items.body:
Daniele Grechi, partner and founder at Grechi Carter Real Estate Lawyers, joins us to talk about how the private and alternative lending space has evolved, and where it’s heading. We look back at the early days of syndicate lending, loose structure and outsized returns, and how the arrival of institutional money since COVID has made private lending far more regulated and competitive.

[00:00] We're meeting a lot of people who are saying, you know, the service we used to get we're not getting anymore. The returns were just absurd for the risk levels. My general thoughts are we're close to the bottom. I think tough times make for better actions. Not every lender is doing every deal anymore.

[00:27] Fergal McAlinden: So, we are joined now by Daniele Grechi who is a partner and founder at Grechi Carter.

[00:34] Grechi Carter. Great to talk to you today. You're in an interesting space to look at how things are going in the mortgage sector and the mortgage industry as a whole. Tell us a little bit about some of the work that you're doing in the mortgage sector at the moment.

[00:46] Daniele Grechi: So, we're still quite busy with the private lending side of things. For us, the really interesting thing has been how the enforcement side of things is growing. There's obviously, with the way the market's been, a real need for that.

[01:00] I think our firm is in a very unique position because we've got a high level of expertise in that space. We've got a full team dedicated, four lawyers, three clerks. So, we can handle a high volume of work and still provide the level of service that our clients would expect.

[01:19] I know that the industry is generally kind of struggling, for lack of a better word. A lot of the big firms in this space have so much volume that we're meeting a lot of people who are saying, you know, the service we used to get we're not getting anymore. That's kind of provided a ton of opportunity for us to spread our wings and grow in this space, and we have.

[01:34] Fergal McAlinden: You mentioned you work in the private lending space. That's obviously seen a big evolution over the past few years. You mentioned that you were last year kind of pre-COVID. What have been some of the big changes that you've seen over the years in terms of how you're working with private and alternative lenders?

[01:46] Daniele Grechi: Well, it's really interesting because we've been in this space for almost 15 years now, and in the first six or seven years, it was such a different space. It was a lot of syndicate lending, a lot less structure, a lot of random different groups, small lenders, and the returns were just absurd for the risk levels that were available.

[02:05] Every year markets were going up 20%. It's sort of an easier space to operate in and because of that a ton of capital flooded to it. Since the COVID era, I think what we've seen is the flock of institutional money through the mix and they very much have professionalized the space.

[02:22] I think what we now refer to as private is kind of institutional, very regulated, very professional, extremely competitive. I think that's sort of the biggest change I've seen since we started in the business.

[02:38] Fergal McAlinden: Looking even to the next year or so, or the next few years, any kind of trends that you foresee? Do you see the space continuing to grow? Are there challenges ahead? What's in store?

[02:47] Daniele Grechi: I definitely think the space is going to grow. I think right now a lot of firms are probably going through some pain because of the change in the market, but a lot of people have adapted.

[02:58] My general thoughts are we're close to the bottom. So, hopefully things are going to move up from here. It's really forced people to have tighter processes. I think tough times make for better actions and people have had to tighten their processes, really look at their underwriting.

[03:14] And I think moving forward I see a more stable space. Opportunities are always going to be there. It's such a big market. I'm just really hoping to see the rebound in the real estate market and that everybody can get busier again.

[03:28] Fergal McAlinden: I think we're all looking ahead to that. Is there anything, Daniele, that you're speaking mostly with brokers about today or any kind of big conversations that you're hoping to have with them?

[03:36] Daniele Grechi: I mean it's always the same types of conversations. They're looking for speed, turnaround, can you handle complicated things? Is there anything different right now than we've seen in the past? No, I don't think there's anything different.

[03:48] Like I said, I think it's that theme of the people who are still working are working hard. It's tougher times, so it's forced people to become better at what they do. And that's kind of the theme right now in the real estate market.

[04:00] Fergal McAlinden: How about the event today? What's your general impressions of how it's gone?

[04:03] Daniele Grechi: A lot of energy. I've noticed a lot of people who are really, really hungry to meet as many people and learn as much as they can.

[04:12] I think it's probably tied into that, you know, not every lender is doing every deal anymore. So, you've got to go to different lenders for different needs. You've got to know your sweet spots for whatever it is that your clients need.

[04:23] So, I do really get the sense that people are here to meet different people, learn about what they do, and see how they can help them with their practice.

[04:30] Fergal McAlinden: Face-to-face conversations, it can't be overstated how important they are.

[04:34] Daniele Grechi: 100%.

[04:35] Fergal McAlinden: All right. Well, good luck with the rest of the event. Great to see you today, Daniele, and we'll talk to you soon.

[04:39] Daniele Grechi: Thanks. Great to meet you.

items.title: Ontario Municipalities Begin Slashing Development Charges As Part Of Federal Deal
items.description:
After reaching an $8.8 billion agreement on March 30 to cut development charges, the Governments of Canada and Ontario have been busy finalizing agreements with local governments to implement the changes.

The initiative is officially known as the Development Charge Reduction Program (DCRP) and applications opened on June 1, as previously reported by STOREYS.

The program “will deliver federal and provincial funding over 10 years for housing-enabling infrastructure projects, with funding prioritized for municipalities that reduce development charges for all residential types by 30 per cent to 50 per cent or greater and maintain the reductions for at least three years.”

Municipalities levy development charges on new construction to fund infrastructure, and this program will see the federal and provincial government fund that infrastructure, allowing municipalities to lower the levies.

The first announcements were made in late-August, with Hamilton receiving $572 million and Vaughan receiving $697.2 million.

Hamilton has committed to eliminating development charges on all residential developments from March 30, 2026 to March 31, 2029, reducing the cost of building new homes by up to $100,442 per home.

The $572 million in funding — with the federal government cost-matching the provincial government — will go toward projects like the widening of Barton Street into a five-lane multi-modal road from Fruitland Road to Fifty Road, widening Rymal Road, widening Garner Road, expanding the Woodward water and wastewater treatment plant, and upgrading the capacity of the Greenhill Water Pumping Station.

A few more announcements were made in September, but the pace of announcements hit another gear this month, with agreements with 11 municipalities announced. To date, agreements announced include:

  1. Hamilton: $572 million
  2. Vaughan: $697.2 million
  3. Bradford West Gwillimbury: $94.8 million
  4. Mississauga: $404.1 million
  5. Barrie: $129.2 million
  6. St. Thomas: $19.6 million
  7. Orillia: $11.3 million
  8. Guelph: $48.3 million
  9. Sudbury: $45.3 million
  10. Essex County: $51.2 million
  11. LaSalle: $25.4 million
  12. Essex Town: $8.8 million
  13. Lakeshore: $11.8 million
  14. Kingsville: $8.4 million
  15. Windsor: $77.6 million
  16. Tecumseh: $6.8 million.

In total, the announcements amount to $2.2 billion in infrastructure funding. In most cases, the agreements will see the local government reduce development charges by 30% to 100% from March 30, 2026 to March 31, 2029.

One announcement that was slightly different was that for Mississauga, whose agreement runs from January 29, 2025 to March 31, 2029, reflecting the fact that Mississauga had previously implemented a development charge incentive program on its own, prior to the Canada-Ontario agreement.

Another announcement that was a bit more unique was that for the County of Essex, whose agreement runs from March 30, 2026 to December 31, 2030. According to the announcement, Essex County is reducing development charges on a staggered timeline. The reduction will be 100% for 2026 and 2027, 75% for 2028, 50% in 2029, and 25% in 2030.

The range of infrastructure projects the $2.2 billion in funding will go towards include road, bus, water, and wastewater infrastructure projects that are described as “housing-enabling.”

Ontario is also home to municipalities that do not levy development charges, however, and the $8.8 billion Canada-Ontario agreement recognizes that as well. In mid-August, the two governments announced a Non-Development Charge Municipalities Stream (Non-DC Stream) that will allow those governments to also receive infrastructure funding that will enable new housing development.

“Municipalities that do not levy development charges often face challenges funding infrastructure projects because they do not have access to this revenue tool,” said the two governments in the announcement. “At the same time, these municipalities face high construction costs, aging assets and significant infrastructure backlogs.”

The Development Cost Reduction Program began accepting applications under the Non-DC Stream on October 29, 2026, with additional intakes expected to be announced at a later date.

The Development Cost Reduction Program is, of course, just one half of the Canada-Ontario deal, with the other being the 13% HST rebate from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027. The HST relief has sparked market activity in certain areas and segments of the market, although the market has still been fairly subdued.

The HST has also been the envy of the real estate industry in British Columbia, which has continued to push for similar relief. The Governments of Canada and British Columbia reached a deal in June that was similar to the $8.8 billion Canada-Ontario deal, but it did not include the tax relief component. The deal did include development charge relief, but the program and agreements were not finalized prior to the snap election held earlier this month.

items.title: Canada’s GDP stalls, clouding Bank of Canada’s December call
items.description: Weak August data and a likely September contraction test the Bank of Canada’s resolve on rates
items.content: <p>Weak August data and a likely September contraction test the Bank of Canada’s resolve on rates</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639289647421852556.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Weak August data and a likely September contraction test the Bank of Canada’s resolve on rates
items.body:
Canada’s economy failed to grow for a second consecutive month in August, and Statistics Canada’s advance estimate for September points to a 0.1% contraction. The outcome lands below the Bank of Canada’s own projections just 48 hours after the central bank’s first rate hike since 2023.

Statistics Canada reported Friday that real gross domestic product was essentially unchanged in August. A 1.4% drop in wholesale trade and a 0.2% fall in the public sector aggregate, its first decline in six months, outweighed gains in retail trade, manufacturing, and construction.

Should the advance September estimate hold, third-quarter annualised growth would reach only 1.3%, against the Bank of Canada’s own 2% forecast.

The Bank raised its overnight rate to 2.50% on October 28, framing the move as risk management against energy-driven inflation. Friday’s GDP data offers a pointed counterpoint.

Benjamin Reitzes of BMO says the Bank of Canada's first rate hike in more than three years may not be its last, with future decisions likely hinging on economic growth, inflation trends, and incoming data over the months ahead. https://t.co/lcW0HncB9d — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 29, 2026

Retail and manufacturing hold the line

Retail trade gained 1.2% in August after contracting in July. Manufacturing rose 0.3%, its fifth increase in seven months, despite continued exposure to US tariffs. Construction added 0.2%.

Against those gains, utilities fell 0.4%, led by a 0.5% decline in electric power generation.

Public administration retreated as 2026 census preparation wound down. Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction were flat.

What the shortfall means for December

Money markets are currently pricing in a hold at the Bank of Canada’s December 10 meeting, followed by a further 25-basis-point increase to 2.75% in January. Friday’s figures complicate that picture.

Marc Ercolao, economist at TD Economics, said the report missed in more than one direction.

“This was a disappointing report relative to expectations and, more importantly, Statistics Canada’s guidance for September looks no better,” he said.

“Taken together, that leaves real GDP growth in the third quarter tracking around 1.3% annualized — still positive, but notably below the Bank of Canada’s recent projection.”

For mortgage brokers monitoring what the BoC’s next decision means for the mortgage market and advising clients through an increasingly complex renewal environment, the gap between growth momentum and Bank projections has become a defining tension heading into year-end.

That concern sits alongside the broader unease felt across the industry since Canada’s rate hike deepened broker worry over a struggling housing market.

Ercolao went further on the Bank’s 2027 outlook.

“For the Bank of Canada, today’s report may cast a little more doubt around the durability of the recovery heading into 2027,” he said.

“The Bank’s latest outlook anticipates a meaningful strengthening in growth next year, but signs of softer momentum heading into Q4 raise the bar for that forecast, particularly with trade uncertainty and higher energy costs still clouding the outlook. While the Bank remains focused on upside inflation risks following this week’s rate hike, weaker underlying growth could complicate the case for further tightening in the near-term.”

The pattern echoes the two straight quarters of GDP contraction in the first half of 2026 that had brokers watching the Bank’s every move, and the second half of the year has yet to deliver the rebound either the Bank or the broker community had anticipated.
